claim: Plasmodium falciparum causes the most severe form of malaria in humans.
source: Plasmodium falciparum causes the most severe form of malaria in humans and is responsible for over 700,000 deaths annually.
evidence: This is stated as established fact in the abstract without supporting data in the manuscript.

claim: Plasmodium falciparum is responsible for over 700,000 deaths annually.
source: Plasmodium falciparum causes the most severe form of malaria in humans and is responsible for over 700,000 deaths annually.
evidence: This is stated as established fact without supporting data in the manuscript.

claim: Plasmodium falciparum is an obligate intracellular parasite.
source: It is an obligate intracellular parasite and invades erythrocytes where it grows in a relatively protected niche.
evidence: This is stated as established biological knowledge.

claim: Plasmodium falciparum invades erythrocytes where it grows in a relatively protected niche.
source: It is an obligate intracellular parasite and invades erythrocytes where it grows in a relatively protected niche.
evidence: This is stated as established biological knowledge.

claim: Invasion of erythrocytes is essential for parasite survival.
source: Invasion of erythrocytes is essential for parasite survival and this involves interplay of multiple protein–protein interactions.
evidence: This is stated as established biological knowledge.

claim: Invasion of erythrocytes involves interplay of multiple protein–protein interactions.
source: Invasion of erythrocytes is essential for parasite survival and this involves interplay of multiple protein–protein interactions.
evidence: This is stated as established biological knowledge.

claim: Binding of parasite invasion ligand families EBLs and PfRhs to host receptors on the surface of erythrocytes is one of the most important interactions in invasion.
source: One of the most important interactions is binding of parasite invasion ligand families EBLs and PfRhs to host receptors on the surface of erythrocytes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge without specific data in this manuscript.

claim: PfRh5 is the only essential invasion ligand within the PfRh family.
source: PfRh5 is the only essential invasion ligand within the PfRh family and is an important vaccine candidate.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge without specific data in this manuscript.

claim: PfRh5 is an important vaccine candidate.
source: PfRh5 is the only essential invasion ligand within the PfRh family and is an important vaccine candidate.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge without specific data in this manuscript.

claim: PfRh5 binds the host receptor basigin.
source: PfRh5 binds the host receptor basigin.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Crosnier et al., 2011 and experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The crystal structure of PfRh5 was determined using diffraction data to 2.18 Å resolution.
source: In this study, we have determined the crystal structure of PfRh5 using diffraction data to 2.18 Å resolution.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PfRh5 exhibits a novel fold comprising nine mostly anti-parallel α-helices encasing an N-terminal β-hairpin.
source: PfRh5 exhibits a novel fold, comprising nine mostly anti-parallel α-helices encasing an N-terminal β-hairpin, with the overall shape being an elliptical disk.
evidence: This is supported by structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The overall shape of PfRh5 is an elliptical disk.
source: PfRh5 exhibits a novel fold, comprising nine mostly anti-parallel α-helices encasing an N-terminal β-hairpin, with the overall shape being an elliptical disk.
evidence: This is supported by structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: This is the first three-dimensional structure determined for the PfRh family of proteins.
source: This is the first three-dimensional structure determined for the PfRh family of proteins.
evidence: This is stated as a factual claim about the novelty of the work.

claim: Plasmodium falciparum is the causative agent of the most severe form of malaria with over 700,000 deaths each year, mostly in sub-Saharan Africa.
source: Plasmodium falciparum is the causative agent of the most severe form of malaria with over 700,000 deaths each year, mostly in sub-Saharan Africa.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The asexual blood cycle of P. falciparum begins with the invasion of human erythrocytes by the merozoite form.
source: The asexual blood cycle of this parasite begins with the invasion of human erythrocytes by the merozoite form of P. falciparum in a complex multistep process involving a cascade of protein–protein interactions between the parasite and host cell (reviewed in Cowman and Crabb, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Invasion of erythrocytes by P. falciparum merozoites is a complex multistep process involving a cascade of protein–protein interactions between the parasite and host cell.
source: The asexual blood cycle of this parasite begins with the invasion of human erythrocytes by the merozoite form of P. falciparum in a complex multistep process involving a cascade of protein–protein interactions between the parasite and host cell (reviewed in Cowman and Crabb, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Invasion of erythrocytes requires members of the reticulocyte binding-like homologues (PfRh or PfRBP) and erythrocyte binding-like (EBL) ligand families.
source: This process requires members of the reticulocyte binding-like homologues (PfRh or PfRBP) and erythrocyte binding-like (EBL) ligand families.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the context of the review citation.

claim: PfRh5 is a member of the PfRh family.
source: PfRh5 is a member of the PfRh family and binds specifically to the receptor basigin on the human erythrocyte surface (Crosnier et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: PfRh5 binds specifically to the receptor basigin on the human erythrocyte surface.
source: PfRh5 is a member of the PfRh family and binds specifically to the receptor basigin on the human erythrocyte surface (Crosnier et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Crosnier et al., 2011.

claim: PfRh5 plays an essential role in merozoite invasion.
source: This protein plays an essential role in merozoite invasion (Baum et al., 2009) and host tropism of P. falciparum (Wanaguru et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baum et al., 2009.

claim: PfRh5 plays a role in host tropism of P. falciparum.
source: This protein plays an essential role in merozoite invasion (Baum et al., 2009) and host tropism of P. falciparum (Wanaguru et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wanaguru et al., 2013.

claim: Polymorphisms in PfRh5 can convert a non-virulent Plasmodium falciparum parasite into a virulent form upon infection of Aotus monkeys.
source: Polymorphisms in PfRh5 can convert a non-virulent Plasmodium falciparum parasite into a virulent form upon infection of Aotus monkeys, supporting the view that this ligand is a determinant of virulence and host specificity (Hayton et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hayton et al., 2008.

claim: PfRh5 is a determinant of virulence and host specificity.
source: Polymorphisms in PfRh5 can convert a non-virulent Plasmodium falciparum parasite into a virulent form upon infection of Aotus monkeys, supporting the view that this ligand is a determinant of virulence and host specificity (Hayton et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by inference from the polymorphism data cited from Hayton et al., 2008.

claim: PfRh5 is a much smaller protein (∼60 kDa) compared to the average of ∼300 kDa for the PfRh family.
source: In particular, PfRh5 is a much smaller protein (∼60 kDa compared to the average of ∼300 kDa for the family) and lacks a transmembrane region.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the protein characteristics.

claim: PfRh5 lacks a transmembrane region.
source: In particular, PfRh5 is a much smaller protein (∼60 kDa compared to the average of ∼300 kDa for the family) and lacks a transmembrane region.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the protein characteristics.

claim: PfRh5 forms a complex with the cysteine-rich protein PfRipr during merozoite invasion.
source: It forms a complex with the cysteine-rich protein PfRipr during merozoite invasion; the complex is peripherally associated with parasite membranes and is released at the apical end of the merozoite during invasion of the human erythrocyte (Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2011.

claim: The PfRh5-PfRipr complex is peripherally associated with parasite membranes.
source: It forms a complex with the cysteine-rich protein PfRipr during merozoite invasion; the complex is peripherally associated with parasite membranes and is released at the apical end of the merozoite during invasion of the human erythrocyte (Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2011.

claim: The PfRh5-PfRipr complex is released at the apical end of the merozoite during invasion of the human erythrocyte.
source: It forms a complex with the cysteine-rich protein PfRipr during merozoite invasion; the complex is peripherally associated with parasite membranes and is released at the apical end of the merozoite during invasion of the human erythrocyte (Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2011.

claim: Antibodies to PfRh5 can block merozoite invasion.
source: Antibodies to PfRh5 can block merozoite invasion, suggesting that it is a potential vaccine candidate (Douglas et al., 2011; Williams et al., 2012; Patel et al., 2013; Reddy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Antibodies to PfRh5 are associated with protection against malaria.
source: This is supported by clinical data showing that antibodies to PfRh5 are associated with protection against malaria, indicating that PfRh5 may be a component of acquired protective immunity (Chiu et al., 2014; Tran et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical data.

claim: PfRh5 may be a component of acquired protective immunity.
source: This is supported by clinical data showing that antibodies to PfRh5 are associated with protection against malaria, indicating that PfRh5 may be a component of acquired protective immunity (Chiu et al., 2014; Tran et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from clinical data cited from Chiu et al., 2014 and Tran et al., 2014.

claim: The full-length 60-kDa PfRh5 protein was expressed in insect cells.
source: Initially, the full-length 60-kDa protein was expressed in insect cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The recombinant full-length PfRh5 protein was capable of binding red blood cells.
source: Although the recombinant protein was capable of binding red blood cells, it was unstable, with the N-terminal region proteolytically degraded to yield a 48-kDa fragment that had a higher erythrocyte binding affinity than that of the full-length protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The recombinant full-length PfRh5 protein was unstable.
source: Although the recombinant protein was capable of binding red blood cells, it was unstable, with the N-terminal region proteolytically degraded to yield a 48-kDa fragment that had a higher erythrocyte binding affinity than that of the full-length protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The N-terminal region of full-length PfRh5 was proteolytically degraded to yield a 48-kDa fragment.
source: Although the recombinant protein was capable of binding red blood cells, it was unstable, with the N-terminal region proteolytically degraded to yield a 48-kDa fragment that had a higher erythrocyte binding affinity than that of the full-length protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 48-kDa fragment of PfRh5 had a higher erythrocyte binding affinity than that of the full-length protein.
source: Although the recombinant protein was capable of binding red blood cells, it was unstable, with the N-terminal region proteolytically degraded to yield a 48-kDa fragment that had a higher erythrocyte binding affinity than that of the full-length protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: PfRh5-C is a highly stable module of PfRh5.
source: We determined the N-terminal amino acid sequence by mass spectrometry and re-expressed this region in insect cells to produce a highly stable module of PfRh5 that we denote PfRh5-C (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: PfRh5-C likely reflects the 45-kDa processed form present in P. falciparum and released into culture supernatant during merozoite invasion.
source: PfRh5-C likely reflects the 45-kDa processed form present in P. falciparum and released into culture supernatant during merozoite invasion (Baum et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with data cited from Baum et al., 2009.

claim: PfRh5-C can bind red blood cells.
source: To show that PfRh5-C is functional, we demonstrated that it could bind red blood cells and the receptor human basigin, which is also produced in insect cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: PfRh5-C can bind the receptor human basigin.
source: To show that PfRh5-C is functional, we demonstrated that it could bind red blood cells and the receptor human basigin, which is also produced in insect cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: PfRh5-C formed a stable complex with basigin as evidenced by size-exclusion chromatographic analysis.
source: PfRh5-C formed a stable complex with basigin as evidenced by size-exclusion chromatographic analysis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The stable PfRh5-basigin complex eluted ahead of free PfRh5 and basigin in size-exclusion chromatography.
source: In these experiments, PfRh5-C was incubated with excess basigin and the stable PfRh5-basign complex eluted ahead of free PfRh5 and basigin (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The stoichiometry of the PfRh5-basigin complex is 1:1.
source: The stoichiometry of the complex was shown to be 1:1 by chemical cross-linking (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The binding affinity of the PfRh5-C–basigin interaction is KD = 43.4 nM.
source: The binding affinity of the PfRh5-C–basigin interaction was determined by surface plasmon resonance (SPR) to be KD = 43.4 nM (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental SPR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The KD value of 43.4 nM for PfRh5-C–basigin interaction is higher than that previously reported.
source: This KD value is higher than that previously reported (Crosnier et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison with previously published data.

claim: A dynamic equilibrium with oligomeric forms within the PfRh5 sample may have contributed to the higher affinity measurement.
source: We note that while the PfRh5 sample used for the SPR measurement was prepared in monomeric form by gel-filtration chromatography, it is possible that a dynamic equilibrium with oligomeric forms within the sample has contributed to the higher affinity measurement.
evidence: This is speculation about possible reasons for the observed measurement.

claim: Antibodies to the recombinant PfRh5-C block growth of 3D7 and W2mef strains of P. falciparum at levels comparable to previous studies.
source: Antibodies to the recombinant PfRh5-C block growth of 3D7 and W2mef strains of P. falciparum at levels comparable to previous studies (Douglas et al., 2011; Bustamante et al., 2013; Douglas et al., 2014; Reddy et al., 2014) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and comparison with cited studies.

claim: PfRh5-C is functionally competent.
source: Taken together, these data imply that PfRh5-C is functionally competent.
evidence: This is inferred from the binding and inhibition data presented.

claim: PfRh5-C was crystallized.
source: PfRh5-C was crystallized and its structure determined through single-wavelength anomalous diffraction (SAD) phasing using iodine-derivatized crystals with subsequent refinement against native diffraction data to a resolution of 2.18 Å (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental crystallographic data.

claim: The structure of PfRh5-C was determined through single-wavelength anomalous diffraction (SAD) phasing using iodine-derivatized crystals.
source: PfRh5-C was crystallized and its structure determined through single-wavelength anomalous diffraction (SAD) phasing using iodine-derivatized crystals with subsequent refinement against native diffraction data to a resolution of 2.18 Å (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental crystallographic data.

claim: The shape of PfRh5-C approximates an elliptical disk.
source: The shape of PfRh5-C approximates an elliptical disk (Figure 2), the core consisting of nine mostly anti-parallel α-helices that encase a small β-hairpin located near the N-terminus (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The core of PfRh5-C consists of nine mostly anti-parallel α-helices that encase a small β-hairpin located near the N-terminus.
source: The shape of PfRh5-C approximates an elliptical disk (Figure 2), the core consisting of nine mostly anti-parallel α-helices that encase a small β-hairpin located near the N-terminus (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Helices α4, α5, α6, and α7 assemble as a triplet-helical coiled-coil domain running the length of the long axis of the molecule.
source: Helices α4, α5, α6, and α7 assemble as a triplet-helical coiled-coil domain running the length of the long axis of the molecule.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Helices α1, α2a, and α3b assemble to form a short three-helix bundle.
source: On the opposite side to the α4/α5/α6/α7 coiled-coil domain, helices α1, α2a, and α3b assemble to form a short three-helix bundle and helices α2b and α3a assemble to form a short two-helix coiled-coil domain, these domains being approximately half the length of the α4/α5/α6/α7 coiled-coil domain.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Helices α2b and α3a assemble to form a short two-helix coiled-coil domain.
source: On the opposite side to the α4/α5/α6/α7 coiled-coil domain, helices α1, α2a, and α3b assemble to form a short three-helix bundle and helices α2b and α3a assemble to form a short two-helix coiled-coil domain, these domains being approximately half the length of the α4/α5/α6/α7 coiled-coil domain.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The α1/α2a/α3b bundle and α2b/α3a coiled-coil domains are approximately half the length of the α4/α5/α6/α7 coiled-coil domain.
source: On the opposite side to the α4/α5/α6/α7 coiled-coil domain, helices α1, α2a, and α3b assemble to form a short three-helix bundle and helices α2b and α3a assemble to form a short two-helix coiled-coil domain, these domains being approximately half the length of the α4/α5/α6/α7 coiled-coil domain.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The 'absence' of a third helix to the α2b/α3a coiled-coil is necessary to accommodate the small β-hairpin in the overall tertiary structure.
source: The 'absence' of a third helix to the α2b/α3a coiled-coil is necessary to accommodate the small β-hairpin formed by residues 161–175 in the overall tertiary structure.
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis.

claim: Within each of the three-helical domains, the central pairwise interactions between the constituent helices are overwhelmingly hydrophobic in nature.
source: Within each of the three-helical domains, the central pairwise interactions between the constituent helices are overwhelmingly hydrophobic in nature.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: The interactions between the helical domains and the β-hairpin are of mixed hydrophilicity.
source: In contrast, the interactions between the helical domains and the β-hairpin and between the α4/α5/α6/α7 coiled-coil domain and the α1/α2a/α3b bundle domain are of mixed hydrophilicity.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: The interactions between the α4/α5/α6/α7 coiled-coil domain and the α1/α2a/α3b bundle domain are of mixed hydrophilicity.
source: In contrast, the interactions between the helical domains and the β-hairpin and between the α4/α5/α6/α7 coiled-coil domain and the α1/α2a/α3b bundle domain are of mixed hydrophilicity.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: The interfaces between helical domains and β-hairpin and between the α4/α5/α6/α7 coiled-coil domain and the α1/α2a/α3b bundle domain are relatively loosely packed.
source: Inspection shows these interfaces to be relatively loosely packed.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: There are two disulfide bonds within the PfRh5 structure.
source: There are two disulfide bonds within the structure.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The first disulphide bond is Cys345–Cys351, located at one apex of the helical bundle.
source: The first disulphide bond is Cys345–Cys351, located at one apex of the helical bundle.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cys345 lies at the C-terminal end of helix α3b.
source: Cys345 lies at the C-terminal end of helix α3b and Cys351 at the N-terminal end of helix α4.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cys351 lies at the N-terminal end of helix α4.
source: Cys345 lies at the C-terminal end of helix α3b and Cys351 at the N-terminal end of helix α4.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The second disulphide bond is Cys224–Cys317.
source: The second disulphide bond is Cys224–Cys317; Cys224 lies close to the N-terminus of helix α2b and Cys317 close to the C-terminus of helix α3a, that is, in proximity to 'kink points' of the parent helices α2 and α3.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cys224 lies close to the N-terminus of helix α2b.
source: The second disulphide bond is Cys224–Cys317; Cys224 lies close to the N-terminus of helix α2b and Cys317 close to the C-terminus of helix α3a, that is, in proximity to 'kink points' of the parent helices α2 and α3.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cys317 lies close to the C-terminus of helix α3a.
source: The second disulphide bond is Cys224–Cys317; Cys224 lies close to the N-terminus of helix α2b and Cys317 close to the C-terminus of helix α3a, that is, in proximity to 'kink points' of the parent helices α2 and α3.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2.

claim: A large loop (residues 240-297) interconnects helices α2b and α3a.
source: A large loop (residues 240-297), located at the opposite apex of molecule to the Cys345–Cys351 disulphide bond, interconnects helices α2b and α3a (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Electron density for residues 258–293 is absent.
source: Electron density for residues 258–293 is absent (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating partial disorder of this loop within the crystal structure.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Residues 258–293 are partially disordered within the crystal structure.
source: Electron density for residues 258–293 is absent (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating partial disorder of this loop within the crystal structure.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of electron density.

claim: Two free cysteine residues (Cys203 in α3 and Cys329 in α4) occur within the structure.
source: Two free cysteine residues (Cys203 in α3 and Cys329 in α4) occur within the structure; the side chain of the Cys329 residue is completely buried, whereas that of the Cys203 is only partly exposed (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The side chain of Cys329 is completely buried.
source: Two free cysteine residues (Cys203 in α3 and Cys329 in α4) occur within the structure; the side chain of the Cys329 residue is completely buried, whereas that of the Cys203 is only partly exposed (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The side chain of Cys203 is only partly exposed.
source: Two free cysteine residues (Cys203 in α3 and Cys329 in α4) occur within the structure; the side chain of the Cys329 residue is completely buried, whereas that of the Cys203 is only partly exposed (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Burial of the free cysteine sulfhydryls is consistent with the monomeric nature of the native protein isolated from parasites and of the recombinant protein.
source: Burial of these sulfhydryls is consistent with the monomeric nature of the native protein isolated from parasites and of the recombinant protein described here.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and biochemical observations.

claim: A search using DALI indicates that the PfRh5 fold is novel.
source: A search using DALI (Holm and Rosenstrom, 2010) indicates that the PfRh5 fold is novel.
evidence: This is based on computational structural comparison using DALI.

claim: The coiled-coil domain formed by helices α5, α6, and α7 is the only element of PfRh5-C found to have a structural homologue within the Protein Data Bank (PDB).
source: The only element of PfRh5-C found to have a structural homologue within the Protein Data Bank (PDB) is the coiled-coil domain formed by helices α5, α6, and α7 (Figure 2): this element can be superimposed with a root mean square deviation of all backbone atoms of 3.4 Å on the N-terminal coiled-coil domain (residues 82–226) of the SipB protein of the bacterial type III secretion system (TTSS) of Salmonella enterica (PDB entry 3TUL, chain A) (Barta et al., 2012) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with the PDB.

claim: The coiled-coil domain formed by helices α5, α6, and α7 can be superimposed with a root mean square deviation of all backbone atoms of 3.4 Å on the N-terminal coiled-coil domain (residues 82–226) of the SipB protein.
source: The only element of PfRh5-C found to have a structural homologue within the Protein Data Bank (PDB) is the coiled-coil domain formed by helices α5, α6, and α7 (Figure 2): this element can be superimposed with a root mean square deviation of all backbone atoms of 3.4 Å on the N-terminal coiled-coil domain (residues 82–226) of the SipB protein of the bacterial type III secretion system (TTSS) of Salmonella enterica (PDB entry 3TUL, chain A) (Barta et al., 2012) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on structural superposition analysis.

claim: Analyses of molecular surface using DoGSiteScorer detected a number of pockets of dimensions suitable for targeting with small molecules on the surface of the PfRh5 structure.
source: Analyses of molecular surface using DoGSiteScorer (Volkamer et al., 2012) detected a number of pockets of dimensions suitable for targeting with small molecules on the surface of the PfRh5 structure.
evidence: This is based on computational analysis using DoGSiteScorer.

claim: These pockets arise from the relatively loose packing of the four constituent domains of the PfRh5.
source: These pockets arise from the relatively loose packing of the four constituent domains of the PfRh5.
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis.

claim: One pocket on the PfRh5 surface is lined by residues of mixed hydrophilicity and has a surface area of ∼430 Å2, of which ∼60% is lipophilic.
source: One of these (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A) is lined by residues of mixed hydrophilicity and has a surface area of ∼430 Å2, of which ∼60% is lipophilic (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: If the identified pocket is in proximity to the basigin binding site, small molecules targeting it may have the potential to interfere with the interaction between PfRh5 and basigin.
source: If this pocket is in proximity to the basigin binding site, small molecules targeting it may have the potential to interfere the interaction between the two molecules, either through disrupting the relatively loose packing of the constituent domains of PfRh5 or through steric interference.
evidence: This is speculation about potential drug targeting opportunities.

claim: PfRh5 functions in complex with PfRipr and at least one further parasite protein.
source: Alternatively, as PfRh5 functions in complex with PfRipr and at least one further parasite protein (Chen et al., 2011), if this pocket is involved in binding these partner/s, a small molecule targeting this pocket may likewise interfere with the complex formation and therefore ultimately with its function.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2011.

claim: If the identified pocket is involved in binding PfRh5 partner proteins, a small molecule targeting this pocket may interfere with complex formation.
source: Alternatively, as PfRh5 functions in complex with PfRipr and at least one further parasite protein (Chen et al., 2011), if this pocket is involved in binding these partner/s, a small molecule targeting this pocket may likewise interfere with the complex formation and therefore ultimately with its function.
evidence: This is speculation about potential drug targeting opportunities.

claim: The reduced and alkylated PfRh5-C has an affinity for basigin with KD = 127 nM.
source: The reduced and alkylated PfRh5-C has an affinity for basigin with KD = 127 nM.
evidence: This is supported by experimental SPR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Reduced and alkylated PfRh5-C shows a threefold reduction in affinity for basigin as compared to untreated PfRh5-C.
source: A threefold reduction in affinity as compared to untreated PfRh5-C (KD = 43.4 nM) was consistent with the two disulphide-bonds being important for the stability of the overall fold of the protein rather than being directly involved in basigin binding.
evidence: This is based on comparison of SPR data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 1C.

claim: The two disulphide-bonds are important for the stability of the overall fold of PfRh5 rather than being directly involved in basigin binding.
source: A threefold reduction in affinity as compared to untreated PfRh5-C (KD = 43.4 nM) was consistent with the two disulphide-bonds being important for the stability of the overall fold of the protein rather than being directly involved in basigin binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the modest reduction in binding affinity upon reduction and alkylation.

claim: A mutant form of PfRh5-C lacking amino acids Asp261–Asn289 was produced in insect cells.
source: A mutant form of PfRh5-C lacking amino acids Asp261–Asn289 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) was produced in insect cells; its binding affinity for basigin was determined by SPR to be 25.9 nM (Figure 3B), that is, comparable to that of the non-mutated PfRh5.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The binding affinity of the PfRh5-C mutant lacking amino acids Asp261–Asn289 for basigin is 25.9 nM.
source: A mutant form of PfRh5-C lacking amino acids Asp261–Asn289 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) was produced in insect cells; its binding affinity for basigin was determined by SPR to be 25.9 nM (Figure 3B), that is, comparable to that of the non-mutated PfRh5.
evidence: This is supported by experimental SPR data shown in Figure 3B.
